title: Enlarged tonsils and adenoids: breathing, sleep and treatment choices
intro: Tonsils sit on either side of the throat; adenoids sit behind the nose. Both are immune tissues that can become large in childhood without being infected. Treatment depends on breathing, sleep, swallowing and hearing difficulties, rather than appearance alone. Many children improve as they grow, while persistent airway obstruction needs assessment.

sections.heading: Notice nighttime and daytime changes
paragraphs: Tell a clinician about regular snoring, mouth breathing, gasping, observed pauses in breathing, restless sleep or unusual sleeping positions. Poor sleep may show up as irritability, overactivity, difficulty concentrating or tiredness. Difficulty swallowing, a persistently blocked nose, recurrent ear problems or concerns about hearing also matter. These symptoms have several possible causes: enlarged tissue is not the same as tonsillitis, and adenoids are not nasal polyps. A brief recording of sleep can help describe the problem, but cannot diagnose sleep apnea.

sections.heading: Arrange assessment and recognize emergencies
paragraphs: Arrange an appointment when symptoms persist or affect learning, eating or sleep. The clinician checks growth, the nose, mouth and ears, asks about allergies and infections, and may refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist. A hearing test or sleep study may be useful. Tonsil size alone cannot establish the severity of sleep apnea. Call 112 for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, collapse or unusual difficulty waking a child. New drooling with inability to swallow or rapidly worsening throat swelling also needs urgent help.

sections.heading: Agree a monitored plan when symptoms are mild
paragraphs: Watchful waiting means agreeing what to observe and when to return, rather than ignoring breathing concerns. Record sleep disruption and changes in daytime behavior, and ask school or nursery whether they have noticed hearing or concentration difficulties. Keep smoke away from the child. A clinician may treat accompanying nasal inflammation, sometimes with a prescribed nasal spray; sprays are not a guaranteed cure for large tonsils. Do not give antibiotics simply because the tissue looks large. Arrange an earlier review if breathing pauses increase, feeding deteriorates or growth becomes concerning.

sections.heading: Discuss what surgery would and would not solve
paragraphs: For troublesome obstruction or established sleep apnea, a specialist may discuss adenoid removal, partial tonsil removal or complete tonsil removal, sometimes together. Recurrent infections are a separate reason for considering surgery. Ask why a particular procedure fits the findings, how much improvement is expected and whether overnight monitoring is needed. Benefits must be weighed against anesthesia, pain, dehydration and bleeding risks. Surgery does not guarantee that snoring, ear problems or sleep apnea will disappear permanently; some children need further sleep assessment afterward.

sections.heading: Prepare for recovery and follow-up
paragraphs: Before surgery, ask for clear instructions about fasting, regular medicines, pain relief, drinking, food and returning to school. Ensure a responsible adult can stay with the child and knows the hospital contact. Follow the discharge plan and do not improvise medicine doses or use leftover antibiotics. Fresh bleeding from the mouth or nose, vomiting blood or breathing trouble after surgery needs emergency assessment, even if bleeding seems to stop. Contact the treating team promptly for poor fluid intake, worsening pain, fever or reduced urination. Review remaining snoring and hearing concerns after recovery.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: snoring with difficult mornings
examples.text: Mira snores and struggles to concentrate at school. Her parent records when she gasps during sleep and asks the clinician about a sleep assessment. The family does not assume that difficult behavior is deliberate or that large tonsils automatically require surgery.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: planning for home recovery
examples.text: Arben is offered adenoid and tonsil surgery after assessment. His caregivers ask about fluids, pain medicine and bleeding. They arrange time off and agree who will seek emergency help if fresh blood appears rather than waiting until the next appointment.

questions: Do the symptoms suggest sleep apnea, hearing problems or another cause, and which tests would help?
Is observation reasonable, and what changes should bring us back sooner?
What are the expected benefits, bleeding risks and recovery needs of the proposed operation?
